steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a Feature Completion Transformer (FCFormer) for occluded person re-identification. Introduce Re-ID and the occluded setting, the main problems it raises and how existing methods address them, then describe our method's components and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Person Re-ID: definition and applications
- Holistic vs. occluded Re-ID
- Three problems of occluded Re-ID
- Existing methods per problem and their shortcomings
- FCFormer: OIL/OIA, dual-stream encoder, FCD, CHT and FC 2 losses
- Contributions list

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Re-ID
  - identify person-of-interest across multiple non-overlapping cameras (cite)
  - applications: video surveillance, activity analysis, sport understanding, tracking
- Holistic vs occluded
  - most methods: holistic Re-ID, body fully visible (cite)
  - real world (stations, airports, shopping malls): occlusion by plants, umbrellas, cars, other pedestrians -> incomplete/invisible body parts
  - occluded person re-identification task proposed (cite)
- Three problems
  - (1) few occlusion samples in training data (cite) -> sensitive to diverse occlusions
  - (2) occlusion noise interferes with feature extraction
  - (3) loss of appearance info -> less discriminative features, wrong semantic alignment (Fig. 1(a), 1(b))
- Existing methods
  - (1) occlusion augmentation strategies (cite); still can't simulate real environment; more samples but not more diversity
  - (2) extra cues (pose estimation, semantic parsing, human mask) for non-occluded parts
    - PGFA: pose info on spatial feature map (cite)
    - PVPM (cite), HoReID (cite): graph-based, node-to-node / edge-to-edge correspondence to mine visible parts
    - external models at inference; sensitive, error-prone with complex backgrounds / severe occlusion
  - (3) GANs predict occluded part at image level (cite); generated regions not convincing, limited performance
    - recent work: feature completion with occluded body part landmarks, region based encoder-decoder, recover from neighboring features (cite); needs extra key-points + predesigned regions, not flexible
- FCFormer
  - adaptively complement features in occluded regions (Fig. 1(c)); four designs
  - OIL: 17 classes of occlusion samples from COCO (cite) and Occluded-duke (cite) training sets
  - OIA: paste patches from OIL -> diverse occluded image pairs; vs random erase (cite) and OAMN augmentation (cite) better simulates real occlusion (Fig. 2)
  - dual-stream encoder: holistic-occluded pairs -> aligned feature pairs; holistic features have more ID representations
  - FCD: self-supervised, learnable completion embedding, supervised by holistic features, no predefined regions or extra labels
  - CHT loss: bridge occluded-holistic feature gap, metric learning
  - FC 2 loss: narrow distribution gap between completion and holistic features in high-dimensional space; self-supervised training of FCD
- Contributions (1)-(4): OIL + OIA; FCD with learnable tokens, no external model, no predesigned regions; CHT + FC 2 losses; experiments on occluded and holistic datasets, favorable vs state of the art

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) is about identifying a person-of-interest across multiple cameras that do not overlap. The task has a wide range of applications in many fields, like video surveillance, activity analysis, sport understanding, and tracking.

In the past few years most existing methods have focused on the holistic person Re-ID problem, which assumes that the pedestrian's body is fully visible. But in real-world scenarios, like stations, airports, and shopping malls, person images from surveillance cameras can easily be occluded by obstacles, e.g. plants, umbrellas, cars, or other pedestrians, and this is a challenge for holistic Re-ID because it has to identify persons with incomplete and invisible body parts. So the task of occluded person re-identification was proposed to solve this problem.

Occluded person Re-ID has more challenges because of three problems: (1) There are only a limited number of occlusion samples in the training dataset, which makes the model sensitive to diverse occlusions. (2) Occlusions introduce a lot of noise information, and this interferes with feature extraction. (3) Occlusions cause appearance information to be lost, so the extracted features are less discriminative and the semantic alignment for matching is incorrect, as shown in Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 1(b).

Many occluded Re-ID methods have been proposed to address these problems. For problem (1), some works focus on designing occlusion augmentation strategies to make the model more robust. But these occlusion augmentation strategies still cannot simulate the real environment well. Many studies stress that it is important to increase the number of occlusion samples during training, but they do not address the need to improve the diversity of occlusions. For problem (2), a large part of the methods use additional cues (e.g. pose estimation, semantic parsing or human mask) to indicate the body parts that are not occluded. For example, PGFA uses pose information directly to indicate non-occluded body parts on the spatial feature map. PVPM and HoReID use graph-based approaches that model topology information by learning node-to-node or edge-to-edge correspondence to mine the visible parts further. These methods directly use external models at the inference stage to extract additional semantic information. But these approaches are sensitive and error-prone when there are complex backgrounds or severe occlusions. For problem (3), some methods try to use GANs to predict the occluded part at the image level, to restore the holistic pedestrian. But the generated regions are still not convincing, so the performance is limited. A recent work does feature completion on occluded regions using occluded body part landmarks and a region based encoder-decoder architecture, which captures spatial information efficiently to recover invisible parts from the neighboring features. But this method still needs extra key-points information and predesigned regions in the feature space, so it is not flexible enough.

- FCFormer: adaptively complement features in occluded regions (Fig. 1(c)); four designs
  - OIL: 17 classes of occlusion samples, COCO + Occluded-duke training sets
  - OIA: paste OIL patches -> more diverse occluded image pairs; better than random erase, OAMN augmentation (Fig. 2)
  - dual-stream encoder: holistic-occluded pairs -> aligned feature pairs; holistic features have more ID representations
  - FCD: self-supervised, learnable completion embedding, supervised by holistic features, no predefined regions / extra labels
  - CHT loss: occluded vs holistic feature gap, metric learning
  - FC 2 loss: narrow distribution gap completion vs holistic features; self-supervised FCD
- Contributions:
  - (1) OIL + OIA, realistic image-level occlusion, robustness
  - (2) FCD, learnable tokens, no external model, no predesigned regions
  - (3) CHT + FC 2 losses: perception and completion ability
  - (4) experiments on occluded and holistic datasets, favorable vs state of the art

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) is about identifying a person-of-interest across multiple cameras that do not overlap. The task has a wide range of applications in many fields, like video surveillance, activity analysis, sport understanding, and tracking.

In the past few years most existing methods have focused on the holistic person Re-ID problem, which assumes that the pedestrian's body is fully visible. But in real-world scenarios, like stations, airports, and shopping malls, person images from surveillance cameras can easily be occluded by obstacles, e.g. plants, umbrellas, cars, or other pedestrians, and this is a challenge for holistic Re-ID because it has to identify persons with incomplete and invisible body parts. So the task of occluded person re-identification was proposed to solve this problem.

Occluded person Re-ID has more challenges because of three problems: (1) There are only a limited number of occlusion samples in the training dataset, which makes the model sensitive to diverse occlusions. (2) Occlusions introduce a lot of noise information, and this interferes with feature extraction. (3) Occlusions cause appearance information to be lost, so the extracted features are less discriminative and the semantic alignment for matching is incorrect, as shown in Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 1(b).

Many occluded Re-ID methods have been proposed to address these problems. For problem (1), some works focus on designing occlusion augmentation strategies to make the model more robust. But these occlusion augmentation strategies still cannot simulate the real environment well. Many studies stress that it is important to increase the number of occlusion samples during training, but they do not address the need to improve the diversity of occlusions. For problem (2), a large part of the methods use additional cues (e.g. pose estimation, semantic parsing or human mask) to indicate the body parts that are not occluded. For example, PGFA uses pose information directly to indicate non-occluded body parts on the spatial feature map. PVPM and HoReID use graph-based approaches that model topology information by learning node-to-node or edge-to-edge correspondence to mine the visible parts further. These methods directly use external models at the inference stage to extract additional semantic information. But these approaches are sensitive and error-prone when there are complex backgrounds or severe occlusions. For problem (3), some methods try to use GANs to predict the occluded part at the image level, to restore the holistic pedestrian. But the generated regions are still not convincing, so the performance is limited. A recent work does feature completion on occluded regions using occluded body part landmarks and a region based encoder-decoder architecture, which captures spatial information efficiently to recover invisible parts from the neighboring features. But this method still needs extra key-points information and predesigned regions in the feature space, so it is not flexible enough.

To solve these problems at the same time, we propose a Feature Completion Transformer (FCFormer) for occluded person Re-ID. The proposed method can adaptively complement the features in occluded regions, as shown in Fig. 1(c). We propose four designs to alleviate the three problems above. First, to get rich occlusion samples, we build an Occlusion Instances Library (OIL) that has 17 classes of occlusion samples taken from the COCO and Occluded-duke training sets. Then we propose an Occlusion Instance Augmentation (OIA) strategy that produces more diverse pairs of occluded training images by pasting image patches from OIL with a specific strategy. As Fig. 2 shows, compared with the existing occlusion augmentation strategies, like random erase and OAMN augmentation, introducing rich occlusion samples simulates real-world occlusion scenarios better. Second, we propose a dual-stream encoder paradigm, which takes the generated holistic-occluded image pairs as input and gets aligned feature pairs. Holistic pedestrian features generally contain more ID representations than occluded pedestrian features. Third, based on this prior information, we propose a self-supervised Feature Completion Decoder (FCD) module to complement the occluded pedestrian features. FCD has a learnable completion embedding representation, and this lets the model complement missing features automatically, under the supervision of holistic pedestrian features, without pre-defining human body regions and without additional labels. Finally, we design a Cross Hard Triplet (CHT) loss for metric learning to bridge the large feature gap between the occluded scene and the holistic scene. We also propose a Feature Completion Consistency (FC 2) loss that explicitly narrows the distribution discrepancy between completion features and holistic features in high-dimensional space, so that FCD can do feature completion and be trained in a self-supervised way.

Our main contributions are:

- (1) We develop an Occlusion Instances Library and an Occlusion Instance Augmentation (OIA) strategy for the Occluded ReID task, which gives more realistic image-level occlusion enhancement and makes the model more robust to various occlusions.

- (2) We propose a Feature Completion Decoder that uses learnable tokens to complete occluded features without help from any external model. Compared to previous completion based works, our method is more flexible since it has no predesigned regions.

- (3) We design a Cross Hard Triplet loss and a Feature Completion Consistency loss to push the model's perception ability and feature completion ability respectively.

- (4) We do experiments on occluded and holistic Re-ID datasets to validate the effectiveness of our method. The results show that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) involves identifying a person-of-interest across multiple non-overlapping cameras [1]. The task has a wide range of applications in many fields, such as video surveillance, activity analysis, sport understanding, and tracking.

In the past few years, most existing methods have mainly focused on the holistic person Re-ID problem [2,3,4], which assumes that the pedestrian's body is fully visible. However, in real-world scenarios such as stations, airports, and shopping malls, person images from surveillance cameras can easily be occluded by obstacles, e.g. plants, umbrellas, cars, or other pedestrians, which makes it challenging for holistic Re-ID to identify persons with incomplete and invisible body parts. Therefore, the task of occluded person re-identification [5] was proposed to resolve this problem.

Occluded person Re-ID faces more challenges because of three problems: (1) The limited number of occlusion samples in the training dataset [6] makes the model sensitive to diverse occlusions. (2) Occlusions introduce a lot of noise information, which interferes with feature extraction. (3) Occlusions cause the loss of appearance information, making the extracted features less discriminative and leading to incorrect semantic alignment for matching, as shown in Fig. 1(a) and Fig. 1(b).

To address these problems, many occluded Re-ID methods have been proposed. For problem (1), some studies [7,8] focus on designing occlusion augmentation strategies to improve the robustness of the model. However, these strategies still cannot simulate the real environment well: many studies emphasize increasing the number of occlusion samples during training but fail to address the need for more diverse occlusions. For problem (2), a large proportion of methods exploit additional cues (e.g. pose estimation, semantic parsing or human mask) to indicate non-occluded body parts. For example, PGFA [6] directly utilizes pose information to indicate non-occluded body parts on the spatial feature map. PVPM [9] and HoReID [10] use graph-based approaches to model topology information, learning node-to-node or edge-to-edge correspondence to further mine the visible parts. These methods directly adopt external models at the inference stage to extract additional semantic information, which makes them sensitive and error-prone when facing complex backgrounds or severe occlusions. For problem (3), some methods [11,12] attempt to use GANs to predict the occluded part at the image level and restore the holistic pedestrian. However, the generated regions are still not convincing, which limits performance. [13] performs feature completion on occluded regions using occluded body part landmarks and a region based encoder-decoder architecture, which efficiently captures spatial information to recover invisible parts from neighboring features. However, this method still needs extra key-points information and predesigned regions in the feature space, which is not flexible enough.

To solve the above problems simultaneously, we propose a Feature Completion Transformer (FCFormer) for occluded person Re-ID. The proposed method can adaptively complement the features in occluded regions, as shown in Fig. 1(c). We propose four designs to alleviate the three problems. Firstly, to obtain rich occlusion samples, we build an Occlusion Instances Library (OIL) containing 17 classes of occlusion samples obtained from the COCO [14] and Occluded-duke [6] training sets. We then propose an Occlusion Instance Augmentation (OIA) strategy that produces more diverse occluded training image pairs by pasting image patches from OIL with a specific strategy. As Fig. 2 shows, compared with existing occlusion augmentation strategies such as random erase [15] and OAMN augmentation [7], introducing rich occlusion samples better simulates real-world occlusion scenarios. Secondly, we propose a dual-stream encoder paradigm, which takes the generated holistic-occluded image pairs as input to obtain aligned feature pairs. In general, holistic pedestrian features contain more ID representations than occluded ones. Thirdly, based on this prior information, we propose a self-supervised Feature Completion Decoder (FCD) module to complement occluded pedestrian features. FCD has a learnable completion embedding representation, which enables the model to automatically complement missing features under the supervision of holistic pedestrian features, without pre-defining human body regions or additional labels. Finally, to bridge the large feature gap between the occluded and holistic scenes, we design a Cross Hard Triplet (CHT) loss for metric learning. In addition, we propose a Feature Completion Consistency (FC 2) loss to explicitly narrow the distribution discrepancy between completion features and holistic features in high-dimensional space, ensuring that FCD can perform feature completion and be trained in a self-supervised manner.

The main contributions can be summarized as follows:

- (1) We develop an Occlusion Instances Library and an Occlusion Instance Augmentation (OIA) strategy for the Occluded ReID task, which provides more realistic image-level occlusion enhancement and effectively improves the robustness of the model to various occlusions.

- (2) We propose a Feature Completion Decoder that exploits learnable tokens to complete occluded features without the assistance of any external model. Compared to previous completion based works, our method is more flexible, as it needs no predesigned regions.

- (3) We design a Cross Hard Triplet loss and a Feature Completion Consistency loss to impel the model's perception ability and feature completion ability, respectively.

- (4) To validate the effectiveness of our method, we perform experiments on occluded and holistic Re-ID datasets. The results show that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods.

References:
[1] L. Zheng, Y. Yang, and A. G. Hauptmann, “Person re-identification: Past, present and future,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1610.02984 , 2016.
[2] Y. Sun, L. Zheng, Y. Yang, Q. Tian, and S. Wang, “Beyond part models: Person retrieval with refined part pooling (and a strong convolutional baseline),” in Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV) , 2018, pp. 480–496.
